finding.claim: The /fetch handler passes the user-supplied `target` query parameter straight to http.Get and returns the response body. There is no scheme, host or IP validation. An attacker can make the server request internal services, localhost or cloud metadata endpoints (e.g. http://169.254.169.254/) and read the responses.
finding.source: HTTP query parameter `target` on GET /fetch (r.URL.Query().Get("target")), controlled by any remote client
finding.sink: http.Get(target) at main.go:16; response body is copied back to the client via io.Copy at main.go:22

trace.note: Route /fetch registered to fetch handler, unauthenticated
target read from the query string with no processing
http.Get(target) issues the outbound request (full-read SSRF)
Response body is streamed back to the attacker; errors are also reflected at line 18

finding.guards_checked: None on this path. The `allowed` host map is only used in safeFetch, not in fetch. No scheme, IP or private-range checks and no authentication. I dropped /safe (safeFetch, main.go:25-38) as a finding: it parses the URL and requires u.Hostname() to be in the allowlist, then requests u.String(), so the host checked is the host requested. Only residual risk is redirects from allowlisted hosts, which is speculative.

verdict.reason: main.go:15-16 passes the unauthenticated query param `target` unvalidated to http.Get and main.go:22 streams the body back (route at main.go:41, no middleware); the allowlist at main.go:27 applies only to safeFetch.
